Think of each group's share of total market value as air pressure. When one group's share rises, others must fall, and the streams show share moving from the groups losing it to the groups gaining it. Click any circle to drill down from sectors to industries to companies.

How it's measured

Method and limits

  • Share comes from price. A group's share of total market value changes by exactly its return relative to the market. Wind is the percentage change in share over the window. Gust is the change in wind compared with the window before it.
  • The explorer uses today's S&P 500 members, grouped by their official GICS sector and sub-industry, with 5 years of daily prices. Company value is price × today's share count, so buybacks and new share issues are ignored. Companies that left the index are missing, which flatters past winners. Share is always measured within the level you are viewing.
  • The stream pairings are illustrative. We know how much share each group gained or lost, but not who sold what to whom.
  • The backtest uses the Fama-French industry portfolios from Kenneth French's data library. These cover every listed US stock since 1926, including companies that later failed, so there is no survivor bias. Their 49 industries are close to, but not the same as, the GICS groups in the explorer. Industry portfolios aren't directly investable. Industry ETFs would add fees and tracking differences.
  • Past results don't guarantee future ones. The effect has been weaker and lumpier since 2000, and momentum strategies have sharp crash years when markets suddenly reverse (1932, 2009, 2024).
